utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we start, is there anything to say by both parties? Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. First of all, I have been informed -- I haven't seen it, but I have been informed that the Trial Chamber granted the motion in respect of a protected witness for closed session and that the Trial Chamber has also decided that it would allow testimony of the witness of events which occurred during the course of a forcible eviction. And I haven't seen the decision, but I'm informed that that was the Trial Chamber's ruling. And so if that is, in fact, the case, Mr. President, then I would proceed along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I can confirm it. We made the decision yesterday afternoon. I believe that soon you'll get the written copies of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Secondly, Mr. President, I have an issue that relates to timing or the order of witnesses. There are a variety of reasons why we're asking for this, but we would ask the Trial Chamber to permit this witness, who I believe will be a pseudonym, MM, that the Trial Chamber permit that witness to testify and to give her direct examination. She is here and would be ready to begin right away. The next witness after her is an open session witness named Jeremy Bowen, and Mr. Bowen has informed us that it would be very important and he would be very grateful if he could finish his testimony today and return to London tonight so that he could return to his job. So we would be asking if the Trial Chamber would permit that the Witness MM give her direct testimony, and then we would then move to Mr. Bowen, who could give all of his testimony, and then we could proceed after that with the cross-examination of Witness MM. That would ensure that Mr. Bowen would be able to finish his testimony today and return to England. And I've asked my learned colleagues on the Defence bench, and I believe that there's no objection from the Defence to proceeding along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have to confirm that from Defence counsels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. That is absolutely correct. We have no objection with that procedure at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good morning. We do agree. We have already given our consent to our colleague Mr. Stringer with regard to this particular sequence of witnesses. We have also received your decision with regard to going into closed session for Witness MM. However, during cross-examination, I would like to say that I will be touching upon all these issues that were mentioned in direct examination, too, so please bear that in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President and Your Honours, I have also read this decision, and I see that pursuant to Rule 93, the Chamber may and can hear testimony of a witness which is capable of establishing a consistent pattern of conduct. I think that is the intent of Rule 93. For the record, Your Honours do not know that this is the sole witness out of 60-some live witnesses and deposition witnesses that will testify about any sexual improprieties during an expulsion, and we believe that the Prosecutor can confirm that. With that in mind, we believe this to be an isolated incident and, therefore, not a consistent pattern. So in that event, we want Your Honours to know that when the time comes, if they choose to ask the witness questions about sexual improprieties, we would still object for the record, for purposes of preserving our objection, because we believe it to be only an isolated incident and therefore not subject to Rule 93. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we have the next witness, I would like to remind both parties, first of all, to Rule 96. We believe that if there is no dispute about that rape incident between the two parties, we hope both the direct examination and cross-examination should be as concise as possible, because the sexual assault was not a charge in the indictment. It's only one form of the pressure the witness and other people received. I hope that both parties will bear this in mind. Yes, Mr. Stringer. Are you ready for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's a closed-session witness, so we'd ask that the blinds are drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could take this opportunity. Where I come from, and perhaps I could suggest, certainly the Prosecution would have no objection if the Trial Chamber were to give both parties on the Defence side a continuing objection on the record so that it's not necessary for them to be on their feet during the direct examination. It's something that's permissible, at least where I come from, under certain circumstances. I haven't seen it here. But in any event, it may also then enable the witness to give that part of her testimony even more concisely without us all dwelling on it if, in fact, the Trial Chamber simply grants the Defence a continuing objection at this time, without requiring them to state their objections at the time the testimony comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree with my colleague Mr. Stringer, Mr. President. In our system also, in our judicial system in criminal proceedings, there is the so-called institute of permanent objection -- continuing objection. So we won't have to rise every time when sexual assault is referred to during the direct examination. So all of us together, notably the witness, should be spared such details as much as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not to repeat myself: In our judicial system, even when someone is accused of a war crime - because that does exist in our legislation - a person cannot be questioned about things that are not included in the indictment. Isolated cases should not be treated at all, and my colleague Mr. Meek pointed out that, and I'm glad to see that there are similarities between our different systems. My continuing objection will be that questions should not be put with regard to isolated incidents, things that do not belong to the indictment. Having said that, we do bear in mind that these are victims and not only witnesses. We bear this in mind all the time. These are people who have suffered. We always keep this in mind. However, we are also only human, and we work very hard all day, and sometimes things happen. We all are aware of comparative international law. If something exceeds the indictment, there is no point in putting questions with regard to that. What Mr. Stringer said yesterday and today, and that is Rule 96 as well, it is consistence, consistence, that shows a continued form of violence. We have not had a single female witness, nor will we have one, who will state that she was abused in this way. Bearing in mind the practice of all the systems we hail from, I believe that the Trial Chamber should not allow this line of questioning at all. That is my continuing objection, our continuing objection that we abide by. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We believe that your objection is correctly recorded in the transcript. And I believe that the Prosecution will bear in mind that the rape is not charged in the indictment. What we want to hear is all the evidence relating to a alleged forced transfer and other forms of terrors asserted to the victims and all that treatment that might have been directed against certain population. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I can inform the Trial Chamber, this witness's testimony is relevant to paragraph 7 of the indictment regarding participation of forces of the army of Croatia. The testimony is also relevant to superior authority under paragraphs 14 and 17. The testimony will be relevant to paragraph 26 of count 1, and also paragraph 54 of count 18, which is the count charging the forcible transfer or forced eviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Which means that you are not going into details of that rape incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to simply ask her to tell us what happened when the soldiers arrived in her flat, and just to -- with the Trial Chamber's permission, really ask her to just tell us what happened. And I agree, there is not a rape count in the indictment. And for that reason, it's not necessary to establish the elements of a crime that one would otherwise have to establish with particular specificity. We don't have to do that in this case, and I don't intend to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Before we say anything about this proposal, I would like to know what this witness has to do with my client and what does this film have to do with this and what does this support in terms of the indictment, which charges, which counts? Because is this supposed to show what happened in East Mostar on some day, some month? I imagine we'll see all of this on this film. I really have no idea what this has to do with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer, would you please brief us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The film was provided to counsel for both accused many months ago, maybe a year or so ago. We invited them at least twice to inform us what was their position in respect of the videotape, whether they would object, whether they would agree, whether it was necessary to even call a witness to testify about it. So counsel I believe is quite well-acquainted with the videotape. I'm prepared to inform the Trial Chamber the specific parts of the indictment which this is relevant to. I can say that this witness is not going to testify directly about either of the accused. He doesn't know either of the accused. But beyond that, it's our view that the videotape, beyond giving evidence - and this witness's testimony will do so as well - of parts of the indictment which are clearly a part of this case, I think that there's nothing better that the Trial Chamber could see than this videotape to see what was the situation in East Mostar during August and September of 1993, which was the period of time in which it was filmed. I think the Trial Chamber is extremely well-positioned to give the various parts of the footage the credibility which they merit viewed in the context of other evidence in this case. But, Your Honour, it's extremely useful evidence, in our view, for the Trial Chamber to see, to have the images of East Mostar and the images of forced evictions taking place during the nighttime, which are shown on this footage. It may be the only footage in this building of war crimes while they are happening. And that's what we propose to show the Trial Chamber in the 40 minutes that it will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to put a very simple question: Could the gentlemen of the Prosecution tell me, or rather, tell the Honourable Trial Chamber and us, these pictures of Mostar, this film from Mostar, what count of the indictment does that refer to? It is true that we received film. Everything that my colleague said is true. And I see no need to emphasise all of that, and there's no denying that. What we are challenging is the following. And of course, I have no influence over Prosecution witnesses, nor would any proposals of mine in this respect be taken into account, and I am not going to go into Prosecution tactics either. I am simply invoking what was said yesterday in this courtroom and what is being said time and again. Obviously it is Prosecution tactics to show as many pictures as possible, to show as many different pictures as possible, those that have to do with the indictment, those that have nothing to do with the indictment, and to create a certain concept, precept even before that. And these things have nothing to do with my client. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as I understand, this film is made about the background of the situation at that time. And we also would like to ask the Prosecutor to show us whether there's any specific counts in the indictment which this film is related to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The evidence of the witness and the film, which we will offer into evidence, is relevant to paragraphs 10 and 11 of the indictment, which relate to the campaign of violence, and also the siege of East Mostar, the shelling and the sniping campaign that was directed at the population that was in East Mostar as alleged in paragraph 10. And also, the evidence will be relevant to count 18, forced evictions, paragraph 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik and Mr. Seric, I can see what your position is and I can see the Prosecution's position. Is it your position that forcible transfer and inhumane treatment to the population of -- the Muslim population of Mostar is denied? You see, if your position is that these terrible things did happen but that your client didn't commit them, that's one thing. But my understanding of the way you've been running this case is not only did your client not commit any of the crimes that were charged against him but these events didn't happen in the way they're described. So perhaps you'd want to check with Mr. Seric about what your position is. Do you deny that the contents of Mr. Bowen's film are true and accurate? And then it becomes an issue. Or do you say there is no dispute but that these things happened? In which case we don't need, probably don't need - I'll have to consult with my colleagues - we wouldn't need to see. You see, if you agree that certain events took place, then there's no dispute. The dispute that we have to determine is whether your client or Mr. Seric's client had anything to do with what happened. Do you see the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour, and thank you for your help. That is precisely what I had wished to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Perhaps a few minutes with your colleagues and then you can come back and let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Seric. I have to apologise. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me the floor. There may have been some misunderstandings amongst ourselves, actually, between my colleague Mr. Seric and me and my partner. There was a point that I wanted to clarify, and my colleague Mr. Meek drew my attention to a problem in the record, in the transcript, that is. I merely wanted to point out that the film that we are about to watch - because, of course, I have already viewed the film - that that film has nothing to do with our clients. As to your question, Your Honour, Judge Clark, I will give you a very brief response. My colleague has his own position. We are starting from the presumption of innocence, of course, and what we deny is the participation of my client in any of these events that we have so far heard about, and that he did not -- our position is that he did not have any knowledge about such events. Because there are things that we hear for the first time from the witnesses here in the courtroom. So that would be briefly my position, Your Honour. Once you see the film, I think my position will become more clear. It concerns a very small portion of the town, that is, the East Mostar, and it was done only from that perspective. We will see images of some people about whom we don't know much -- actually, which don't know anything at all. We don't know who there are, by whom they had been expelled, and from where. And my colleague Mr. Meek has justly pointed out the fact that the images we're going to see have nothing to do with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I have now been involved in this without any reason. I did not make any representations as to this video footage. I am not opposed to the viewing of this film. As for the position of this Defence team, ever since the first day, I think our position was clear, and it can be encapsulated in the not guilty plea of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Of course, that your clients will be presumed innocent before the convictions made by this Trial Chamber. We fully agree with you. As for your interventions, both of the Defence counsel said that you do not oppose to seeing this film by us. So anyhow, before we see that film, we couldn't know what this film is about, so we are going to hear the next witness, and we are going to watch that film. So decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We call Jeremy Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: May the usher bring that witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure what are your intentions now in terms of the lunch break, because we started a little early. If we go until 1.00, the normal time, I believe we could actually get through the introductory comments, as well as the videotape itself, before the lunch break without having to interrupt the videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll finish that section before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, your name and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It's Jeremy Bowen, and spell it B-o-w-e-n.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you employed, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I work for BBC. Can I turn down the volume on my earphones a little bit? It's very loud. Okay. I work for the BBC. I'm a journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Currently, your current duties as a journalist, what does that entail?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm a news anchor for the BBC. I present the main BBC morning news show on the main network, BBC1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, before you continue, I would ask you to keep in mind - both of us need to keep in mind - that as we speak, interpreters behind us are translating and interpreting our words into other languages, so that we're going to need to speak slowly and to try to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, could you please just give us a background about your experience as a journalist with the BBC.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I joined the BBC in 1984 after I finished at university. I was a trainee on their graduate training programme, which I did for a couple of years. In 1987, I had my first foreign posting for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we would stipulate to this background -- so we can go right into the film, we would stipulate to this background that he's a newsman and has credentials to make such a documentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Take 30 seconds. I think the witness just ought to be able to tell us about his background. I'm going to bring this down to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, which I think is particularly pertinent to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll hear what happened in the former Yugoslavia at that time, but you will make it as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, let me ask you just a couple of particular questions. You said that you joined the BBC in 1984 in the training programme. Let me ask you, in the years since then, have you covered armed conflicts in various parts of the world?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. I describe myself as a very experienced war correspondent coverer of armed conflict. I started doing it in 1989 in El Salvador. I covered Afghanistan the same year. I covered the Romanian revolution. I was in Baghdad during the Gulf War when it was being attacked by the allied side. I started covering the wars of former Yugoslavia in 1991 with the Croatian war in Eastern Slavonia, Vukovar. I was in Vukovar quite a bit while it was being shelled. I covered that war extensively during the summer and early autumn of 1991. I started covering the war in Bosnia in July of 1992 in Sarajevo. I spent a lot of that summer in Sarajevo. In the later part of that year, September -- from September, I covered the situation in Central Bosnia, the Lasva Valley, Kiseljak, Travnik, Busovaca, Vitez, places like that. I was in Sarajevo again over the winter and right through 1993 until August of that year, when I heard about the situation in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then subsequently, were you involved in making a documentary about the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us -- we're going to play it in a few minutes. Could you tell us how this came about.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. In August of 1993, I was in Sarajevo covering the situation there. I was at a briefing giving by the UNHCR, by their spokesman Peter Keslar, and he said that there was a very difficult situation in the eastern part of Mostar where upwards of 20.000 Muslims were besieged. He said that there was a path into the east side of Mostar which the Bosnian army were using to get weapons in and supplies. So I thought this was going to be a very important story, and I found out how to do it. I had to get quite extensive permissions to get down there. And I went in on foot with the Bosnian army from Jablanica, walked across the mountains, and I was in there for August of that year for a week or ten days. When I got back to London, I produced -- a colleague of mine at the BBC said that he wanted to make a documentary about Bosnia, and what should he do it about. I said, "Look, I've just been in Mostar. There's an incredible situation going on there. We should go there and make a documentary." So we worked towards doing that, and we went in to film in September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Mostar in September approximately?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Approximately three weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then subsequently, then, in the months that followed, the documentary was produced, or made?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was aired, I think, in November of '93 on the BBC. It was also aired on ABC "Nightline" in the States and I think in various other countries where the BBC syndicated it around the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, the footage, the images which appear in the videotape, the documentary, when were those filmed?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The images were filmed mainly in September of 1993 and in the early part of October as well, actually. We were still there in early October. Some of it was -- a couple of sequences were filmed in August, in our trip in August. But the vast majority of it was filmed during our three weeks or so in the city in September and October 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would propose to play the videotape, which should be in the technical booth marked as Exhibit 586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It might be useful to turn down the lights as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: JEREMY BOWEN: Croatian propaganda echoing over the front line in Mostar, the most vicious theater of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since May, Bosnian Croats, aided and abetted by the Croatian government, have been laying siege to about 60.000 people in East Mostar. Almost all of them are Muslims and they are fighting back hard. There are no safe places in East Mostar. You can be killed or maimed at any time on any street corner. Until you see it happening, it's hard to realise how quickly lives can be destroyed. Franjo Pavlovic [phoen], who was born a Croat, made the mistake of going out to repair some shell damage on what had started out as a quiet morning. Because Raima, his wife, is a Muslim, the Croats expelled them over the front line into East Mostar in August. He had one chance. A fire engine, the only one left on this side of Mostar, was nearby. Perhaps it could get him to the hospital in time. Nothing in her life before the war had prepared Mrs. Pavlovic for this. She is 53. After they married, she worked as an accountant in a graphic design business. The last traces of that life disappeared when her husband was hit. The streets were empty, and not just because of the shelling. There is a six-hour-long daytime curfew. The idea is to stop people getting hurt. The hospital was only a few minutes away. Nothing is more than a few minutes away in East Mostar. The doctor hardly had to look at him. Mr. Pavlovic was dead. He had been killed by shrapnel in the chest. For her sake, he went through the motions. RAIMA PAVLOVIC: [Foreign language] JEREMY BOWEN: "You haven't examined him yet," she said. "Please do more." Everything, from the explosion to this, had taken about ten minutes. The hospital was ready for the next casualties. RAIMA PAVLOVIC: [Voiceover] This morning we were trying to repair our wall. It was destroyed by a mortar. He stepped out to find out what the time was and to get some water so that I could wash our clothes. That's when it happened. JEREMY BOWEN: The more the doctors see, the more it hurts. They said they try not to let it show. They had been married for 32 years. The River Neretva cuts Mostar in two. These wrecked buildings are on the east bank, the stronghold of the Muslim-led Bosnian government forces. But they have an important foothold on the otherwise Croat-controlled west bank as well. To get there, you have to cross the old bridge, which was built in the 1500s. It's been hit many times, but it's still standing, just about. The Croats on the hill know that if the bridge falls, they will have savaged morale on the other side. It would be a strategic victory as well, because it's the route to the front line. A local cameraman, called Miralem Smailhodzic [phoen], documented the Croat's attempts to destroy it. He took these pictures. He is dead now, killed by a mortar a month or so ago. They were bringing bodies back from the front the day that we first crossed. The stretcher bearers worked for a well-organized civil defense network. Men who aren't in the army have to take part. East Mostar, because it's so isolated, has become the Bosnian government's best-run and most highly mobilised enclave. It has to be, because they have so little. They had to hope that the blankets would hide them from the snipers. You can't move very fast when you are carrying a stretcher. Normally they don't bother to bring the dead this far, but this man was alive when they started the journey and they wanted to try to get him to the hospital. There didn't seem much point in turning back when he died. The soldiers told us that the best way across is to run. This is the least dangerous way over the River Neretva. A stroll across here used to be recommended in all the tourist guides. One other bridge still stands, but it's even closer to the Croat positions. MALE: Croatian front line fifty meters from us. JEREMY BOWEN: The soldiers' morale is surprisingly high even though they're out-gunned by the Croats. They use pieces of broken mirror to look at their enemies in the way that soldiers of another generation used periscopes in the trenches. War has its routine: standing guard, hanging around, often under fire. That was a rocket-propelled grenade hitting the floor above. Another exploded in the building opposite. As usual, the Bosnian army here is short of weapons, so they make their own. They call this one "little thunder." The explosive, they said, came from unexploded Croat bombs. JEREMY BOWEN: What is it like now in Mostar to be a soldier? SOLDIER: We are all soldiers now here, and it's an ordinary life. JEREMY BOWEN: It sounds like a tough life. SOLDIER: Yes, it's a very tough life. It's a very tough life. JEREMY BOWEN: So far, except for the Tanoys relaying Croat propaganda, not all that different from any other urban front line in Bosnia-Herzegovina, even down to the bodies rotting in no man's land. But it is different, because the Bosnian government soldiers here are learning. They are certain they have gained the edge over their Croat enemies on the other side of the line. Everything they have suffered since the war started has made one essential fact very clear: If they are going to survive, it's down to them. Nobody is going to come to the rescue. The people here are surrounded by enemies, and long ago they stopped dreaming about international military intervention. But they think they can win this war because they have nowhere else to go, because their suffering has made them strong, and because they believe they have a simple choice: to fight or to die. The first rule of movement in Mostar is to keep out sight of the Croat gunners on Hum, the hill which dominates the city. The second is don't slow down, or the Croats on Hum will pick you off, if their colleagues beyond the sandbags and down the street don't get you first. The Bosnian soldiers here know all about that, and much more. If they didn't, they wouldn't have survived this long. This unit's commander is Nermin Brkan, a 31-year-old who was a veterinary surgeon before the war. He used to specialise in animal reproduction. Now, like his colleagues, he's learned how to kill. This homemade bomb, they complain, was too heavy to throw. They prefer the smaller ones. NERMIN BRKAN: I don't like it, shooting anybody, but I must. I must, we think, because enemies on other side. I live here, live here my father, my mother, my grandfather, my grandmother, dead here. I am living here. I am fighting for this my house, for my parents, for my colleagues, for my people, for my country. JEREMY BOWEN: Would you accept a peace settlement that said Mostar will be a divided city like Berlin? NERMIN BRKAN: Like Berlin? JEREMY BOWEN: Berlin, yeah, before the wall came down. Would you like Mostar to be like that? NERMIN BRKAN: No. No. No. JEREMY BOWEN: And if you lose, where do you go? NERMIN BRKAN: I don't know. I don't know. JEREMY BOWEN: Refugees started appearing in no man's land. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts – Pages 5779 to 5789. NERMIN BRKAN: Oh, another man, old man and old woman. JEREMY BOWEN: He told them to hurry and to take cover. Often the Croats start shooting once they've forced Muslims out of West Mostar through this section of the front line. Fatima and Salim Matic [phoen] had just been thrown out of their home by Croat gunmen. Mr. Matic, who is 72, managed to put on three shirts and to grab two umbrellas as he left. His wife, who is 70, was still in her nightclothes. Their neighbor, 84-year-old Mrs. Almasa Humo, arrived a few minutes later. "Don't sit there," they told her. "They could kill you." Even if Mrs. Humo still cared, she didn't have the strength to move any further on her own. The soldiers see the old and the weak arriving like this every day. They have heard so many accounts of brutality, inhumanity and dispossession that they can hardly bear to listen anymore.

utterances.speaker: MRS. HUMO
utterances.text: [Foreign language] JEREMY BOWEN: She said the Croats had slapped her so hard that her cheeks still hurt. The soldiers say they're Bosnians first, Muslims second, but all the suffering is sharpening their Muslim identity.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MATIC
utterances.text: [Foreign language] JEREMY BOWEN: "The Croats hate us because of our religion," she said. But for the soldiers it's not a religious matter; it's a question of power, of protecting their own people, people like the women and children expelled from West Mostar. This family were lucky. The Croats were only trying to scare them. NERMIN BRKAN: This here war, it's only war. JEREMY BOWEN: Just guns? NERMIN BRKAN: Just guns. JEREMY BOWEN: No human rights? NERMIN BRKAN: No. No. You see? Human rights? Human rights? Body, killing people, fight woman and children. It's your human rights? Two hundred thousand people, Muslim, die. When, when, when stop? When justice? Where, where is justice? Where? Who die, die. Who live, live. JEREMY BOWEN: The lesson the soldiers have drawn from the ethnic cleansing is that if you want to live, you have to fight. The refugees were led off into the heart of the enclave, where no civilian would disagree with the soldiers' conclusions. East Mostar has organised itself for a long war. In charge of that are Mostar's military leaders. In the chair, Esad Humo, an architect before the war. Like all East Mostar's commanders, he's found that he has a talent for fighting, leadership, and survival. Nobody in the room said they wanted a Muslim state, but nobody denied they were fighting for Muslim rights. COLONEL ESAD HUMO, MOSTAR BRIGADE: Two years ago I was normal, if I can say normal. Normal citizen working, you know, learning. I had a job, wife, kids, brother, home. Now everything is changed. JEREMY BOWEN: Tell me, what are you guys here fighting for? ESAD HOMO: For what we are fighting? At first, for a place for living. For surviving, that's what we are fighting for. That's first thing, and after that comes something else. JEREMY BOWEN: What comes after that? A Muslim state? ESAD HUMO: Hmm, Muslim state. I am not sure, because I am not fighting for a Muslim state. I am fighting for a state, I can say the same as England or same as the French, I mean state for the people who can live together without any difference. JEREMY BOWEN: Do the experiences you've had over two years affect the way that you fight? ESAD HUMO: We learn how to kill, yes. Not only, not only the soldiers; people learn how to survive. Because here is law of jungle. If you don't want to be killed, you should kill. That's normal jungle law. It's -- everybody knows about that. JEREMY BOWEN: Jungle law, in conditions unfit for animals. "All we have left," these women say, "is sadness and pain." One gave us a letter to take out to a world they think has abandoned them. The civilians know that their only hope is to help themselves, to hang on until the killing ends, to survive the winter. But how do you avoid pneumonia, bronchitis, and worse, when shells have smashed your roof? These people are refugees. They live in a ruin, like thousands of others in East Mostar. She can't walk. She lies in stinking clothes on a soaking bed. MALE: [Voiceover] What can I do? Either I die or go on living like this. JEREMY BOWEN: Do you think your army will come to rescue you to, to win this war for you? HEMALINA TANOVIC: Yes. JEREMY BOWEN: Why is that necessary? Isn't it better to talk? HEMALINA TANOVIC: I think it's necessary because there's no use, not any use of talking with them, because they -- they don't want to live with us. JEREMY BOWEN: But it will take the Bosnian army to free you. It won't be the outside world or negotiations; it's your soldiers who will do it? HEMALINA TANOVIC: Yes, because I want to tell you: We, we really don't trust anyone, because everybody talking about us, talking about hard situation, difficulty of life, but no one does anything. JEREMY BOWEN: Most people only go out when they have to, once a day to the soup kitchen. Each container full has to last a family 24 hours. There isn't much, but they all get about the same. The black market which has corrupted Sarajevo doesn't exist in East Mostar. Because hardly any aid gets into the city, there is nothing to buy or sell. It's all rationed. The civilians do as they're told. They have no choice. Organisation begins at the front line. They've set up forward first aid stations. Nusreta Becic [phoen], who used to be a geologist, is in charge of this one. She runs it from her own home. She was treating one of her neighbors when there was another explosion. It was very close, even closer than they thought. Two men had been walking down the street. A lot of people live in this area. It's only a few hundred yards from the Croat positions. She slapped the man who was most seriously wounded to try to stop him going into shock. Passersby ran to help. Somebody shouted for some water. The man on the right died. They managed to save the other man. Not long afterwards, another emergency. A woman was lying on the river bank. She had been doing her family's washing. She was already dead, shot by a Croat sniper. If they survive long enough, the wounded are brought here to the hospital. It's another favorite Croat target. The stretchers are taken into the cellar of the building which used to be a public health laboratory. The hospital director is Dr. Dragan Milavic. He set it up from nothing just before the war with the Bosnian Croat army, the HVO, started. Mostar's modern infirmary, where he used to work, is on the Croat side. This is a charnel house, but it's all they have. The corridor smells of blood. It isn't remotely sterile. There isn't enough space for the wounded. East Mostar is a small place. Often they treat people they know. Sometimes they treat people they love. SELMA SLJIPEVICIC [phoen]: I ran out in the hall and I saw -- I saw my father lying on the floor, on stretchers. I looked at his face. One eye was open, one eye was closed, and he didn't have this side of his face, and I could see his teeth. And in that moment, I thought: It's okay. It's only face. They can fix it. He'll have a scar. So what? He doesn't have to be beautiful. And I looked down, and I uncovered him, and I saw huge hole here. He wasn't bleeding. It was just a red hole. And I tried to, to, to touch the shrapnel. You're used to do it when you work in a hospital. Then you touch, you -- to establish where the shrapnel is. Is it deep inside or is -- I, I start doing it and my hands were full of my father's blood. DRAGAN MILAVIC: [Voiceover] We face huge problems, but we realise we have to solve them ourselves. We have to sort things out by ourselves. Whenever I talk to the Red Cross or Medecins Sans Frontiere, or any other international organisation, they tell me, "We would help you, but our actions are limited by the Croat HVO forces besieging the city." They always mention the HVO. They use them as an excuse for their own limitations. JEREMY BOWEN: The result is that Emir Demic is watching his 12-year-old brother Armele die. He is with him all the time. Armele has been in a coma since he was hit in the head by shrapnel. Sometimes he looks a little better, almost as if he could be coming round. Like promises of medical evacuation, it's a cruel deception. EMIR DEMIC: [Voiceover] He's got no real chance here, and the doctors are saying that every moment is precious. JEREMY BOWEN: Has anybody said that he might get evacuated? EMIR DEMIC: [Voiceover] Some promises have been made, but they are empty promises. DR. DRAGAN MILAVIC: [Voiceover] A large number of patients have died because we don't have the facilities to treat them properly. Under these conditions, I don't think the kid stands a chance. JEREMY BOWEN: It never stops. Eleven-year-old Medina has just been wounded in the head. A shell hit her family's flat. The hospital didn't have a bed for her, so they left her on a stretcher. Her father wasn't much bothered by his own shrapnel injuries, which were serious enough. All he could think about was his daughter. They were preparing her for an operation. Seven months ago, the theater was an empty storeroom. They have a brain surgeon at the hospital who didn't want to be filmed because his wife and child are on the other side. But the only diagnostic aid he has is an old x-ray machine, so he can't do much. Dr. Milavic, the hospital director, is also the anaesthetist. He sedated Medina and they started work. International donors have promised him a modern field hospital, much better than the primitive conditions here that they all loathe. But the hospital is stuck in Croatia. Nobody seems capable of getting it to East Mostar. They didn't try to take the shrapnel out of Medina's brain. It was too risky. Her only chance was evacuation to a proper hospital a long way from the war. There was an explosion. A shell had landed just outside the hospital. A doctor who'd gone to the top of the stairs leading down to the cellar had been wounded. It's dangerous to stand there, but they do, to get away from the fetid atmosphere downstairs. "Give me some space," Dr. Milavic said. He'd rushed out of the operating theater to examine his colleague. The wife of a hospital worker who was slightly wounded was helped down. The injured doctor was scared. Bad leg wounds often end in amputations in this hospital. Dr. Milavic tried to reassure him. He had been lucky, by the standards of this place. The doctors are at breaking point. It's not unusual for one man to perform ten major operations in a day. A few yards away, the operation on Medina was still going on. They had time to do the best they could for her. No other casualties had come in. It gets no better at night. Five hundred Muslims had just been robbed and thrown out of their homes in West Mostar by the Croats. They had to cross the River Neretva to get to comparative safety on a bridge made of rope and planks. Bosnian soldiers told them which way to go. The Croats were shooting at the people they'd just made refugees. Only a few hours before, until the Croat gangs had come for them and forced them over the front line, they'd thought they were safe. They had been settling down for the night. The Croat machine-guns didn't let up, and the refugees kept on coming. They were trying to kill old men and women, mothers and their children. She was so frightened she could barely walk, but she tried to calm her sons. Each new family has to be fed and housed. This is a war crime with a cold purpose: to increase the pressure on the military authorities in East Mostar. The brutality of the expulsions drives home the message that compromise with Croat extremists is neither possible nor desirable. The refugees spent their first night in East Mostar in a bombed-out theater. In one evening, all of them had lost their homes and possessions. They talked of persecution, rape and murder. FEMALE: [Voiceover] We were driven to a small wood. My sons were pulled out of the car. They were taken into that wood. I was told that their throats were slit. I only live because I have to, only because I have to. What sort of life is this? ANOTHER FEMALE: [Voiceover] What do I know about politics? I have never thought about it. Tonight the Croat soldiers told me to shut up, to be quiet. That's what I did. I have never done anything to anyone. JEREMY BOWEN: The next morning a corpse was lying where the refugees had crossed. It was a woman in a pink sweater. A shopping bag was on either side of her. The UN is examining documents that one of the refugees smuggled out in his shoes. He didn't want us to show his face. He said they were lists of the names of dead Muslims he was forced to bury. Some were civilians, some were soldiers. In all, there were 274 names. A woman said that ten men raped her and robbed her before she was expelled. FEMALE: [Voiceover] My mother whispered to me, "They'll kill us." I just said to her, "Don't be afraid," very quietly, so they couldn't hear me. I thought that they were going to shoot us, that they'd rape me and kill me afterwards. Luckily, they didn't kill me -- well, lucky as far as being killed is concerned. But the rape ... Sometimes my brain simply stops working. I can't get my thoughts together. I am fighting on my own. It's difficult. JEREMY BOWEN: Buildings can be restored, but every rape and every killing, and the destruction of their city, is changing these people. Goran Stosic was our guide on a particularly nasty section of the front line. He was crouching because the Croats were shooting from their positions on the other side of the wall. To survive and to win, they are doing things of which not so long ago they wouldn't have dreamt. Goran has become an accomplished fighter. Before the war he was trying to qualify as a lawyer. He talked about a country where Muslims, Serbs, and Croats could live together again. After all, he pointed out, there are still Serbs and Croats in the Bosnian army. We moved slowly along the river bank, out of sight of the snipers, but they could see us on the way up to the trenches. It makes no difference that some Serbs and Croats are in the Bosnian army. Most of the rest aren't. Any chance of reconciliation was lost in trenches like this long ago. There will be no going back to what they had here once for at least a generation. Hodza, Goran's commander, used a mirror to point out the whereabouts of a Croat sniper. He was in the tower. Hodza didn't try to hide the way the Bosnian army treats its prisoners either. A Croatian prisoner of war appeared in the trench we just crossed. Prisoners dig the trenches and lay sandbags in the most exposed and dangerous positions on the front line. When they are not working, they are imprisoned in a sweaty, badly ventilated cellar. We could film, but we weren't allowed to talk to any of them. One prisoner was badly wounded. He was in considerable pain. A lot of the prisoners had been hurt. The injuries were caused, their guard said with some relish, by Croat fire on the front line. The prisoners were thin, but they looked no worse fed than many civilians in East Mostar. The guard said they eat the same food. Their captors know that the work they do on the front line - here they were exhuming bodies - contravenes the Geneva Convention. As far as they're concerned, though, that's better than seeing their own people doing it. In this war there is no middle way. There are victors and there are victims. The Bosnian soldiers know which they want to be. They dug up these bodies to use them as currency in a prisoner exchange. Mostar is the most devastated city in the former Yugoslavia, worse than Sarajevo or Vukovar. It's a vicious fight, and it has a long way to go. Hodza commands the Bosnian Army in Santici, the old commercial district. Its backyards, basements and alleyways are where the heaviest fighting in Mostar happens. In Santici, the Bosnian Army is putting its new hardness to the test. The soldiers have found that in these urban battlefields, you end up dead if you hold back, if you hesitate to kill. That means no pity and no mercy. Hodza told us that Croats make Bosnian army prisoners work on the front line too. Sometimes they make them build positions only a few feet away. Hodza said they have seen prisoners who are friends, cousins, even brothers. The sandbags mark the Croat HVO lines. But the orders are clear: Attack, even if Bosnian prisoners are in the way. EFTAN TIKVESA: [Voiceover] The enemy were very close. We pushed forward our positions. Only a wall about twenty or thirty centimeters thick separated me from two HVO soldiers. They were using our prisoners, making them work at gunpoint. I had to throw two hand grenades in among them. JEREMY BOWEN: Away from the fiercest fighting, the Bosnian army also controls the outlying villages to the north and the south. General Arif Pasalic, the regional commander, took us to see them. He is a professional soldier. He was an officer in the JNA, the old Yugoslav army. Shells came in from the Croat side occasionally, but it was a quiet day. The Bosnian positions were secure. Even Mostar itself, five miles away, was fairly calm. The general, though, was not a happy man. He should have been. In thirty hours of intense combat, his men had battled their way through a Croat-controlled suburb and up the mountain called Hum, which dominates Mostar. It was probably their single most significant victory of the war. ARIF PASALIC: [Voiceover] That mountain is the key, whether you are attacking or defending. Whoever wants to conquer Mostar must take control of the mountain, and whoever defends Mostar must keep control of the mountain, because it dominates the city and the whole of the valley. JEREMY BOWEN: But the order came from Sarajevo saying they had to retreat. The government wanted to send a positive signal to the peace talks. The general complied reluctantly, but he refused to go to Sarajevo for consultations about the talks, a process in which he had no faith or interest. Sarajevo controls the pack horses which resupply East Mostar with ammunition, so it still calls the tune. But just in case, though, the independent-minded Mostar commanders are buying weapons from the Serbs as well. The route across the high mountains will be much harder during the winter. Our convoy waited until it was dark before attempting the most difficult part of the journey, first on foot, through an opening in the Croatian front line. On the outskirts of Mostar they transfer the ammunition into vehicles, then move at speed down a contested road. The Bosnian army controls the tarmac, but the Croats have mounted searchlights alongside it. Their positions are a few hundred yards from the road. There is always the hope that if you drive fast enough, the searchlight operators won't be able to pick you up. We were unlucky. It was a tense few moments. Each vehicle only carries a small amount of ammunition in case it is hit and they lose the consignment. There is another route into Mostar, the main road. UN convoys use it when the Croats let them. Food lorries are so rare here that their arrival always cause a stir. This time they delivered a load of flour. The soldiers and then the hospital take most of what is brought in. Ordinary civilians come a very poor third. There isn't enough. They all face a hungry as well as a dangerous winter. The convoy brought a UN medical team to the hospital as well. They came to work out which cases were serious enough to be evacuated abroad. Dr. Milavic took them to the two children with head wounds. MALE: Here, is this the one? JEREMY BOWEN: Emir Demic was still at his brother's bedside. He had been waiting desperately for this. He had spent most of the last two weeks with Armele, who was still in a deep coma. A few feet away lay Medina. FEMALE: [Voiceover] I'd like to take my child out of this madness. This is hell. If only she'd wake up. JEREMY BOWEN: But Medina's condition was deteriorating. She died a little later. The funeral was held after dark because of snipers. Medina wasn't evacuated in time because both sides use medical evacuation as a weapon of war. They weren't prepared to make a deal for her, for Armele, who was still alive when we left, or for anybody else. The fight is all that matters now in Mostar. They have grasped the cruel essence of this war: that compromise counts for nothing, that only the strong will survive. JEREMY BOWEN: What if your military efforts are undercut by President Izetbegovic signing a piece of paper that says: "We have a cease fire just where we are now and we stop fighting"? Would you accept that? ESAD HUMO: He will not do it. You understand what I mean? He will not do it, so no talking about that. No way. It's not -- there is not any possibility that he or anybody else can say: It's finished. Your town is divided or you will leave the town. JEREMY BOWEN: A lot of your men have been killed here. Your own brother was killed fighting. How much longer can you go on taking these losses? How much longer can you see your men being killed? Because they are not going to all last forever, are they? ESAD HUMO: You know, I think that it's -- sorry, but for me it's the wrong question, and I know only the right answer on that wrong question. The right answer is: We will win. That's the answer. It's not the question how long. I don't know how long. Next ten years, next twenty years. I don't know. I understand what you ask, but you should try to understand me, that we will fight to the end. SOLDIERS: [Singing] JEREMY BOWEN: These young men - Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, all soldiers in the Bosnian army - are singing about the death of Mostar, the city where friendships like theirs were possible. They hope their children will be friends. That's if they live long enough to become fathers.
