utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, a few moments ago I was reminded and asked if we could maybe speak a little more slowly and pause just a little longer --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in between question and answer. Now that we've seen the documentary which you made, I wanted to ask you just a few questions about it. At the beginning, you state that Mostar at that time, I think you said, was the most vicious theatre of fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I wanted to ask you to what extent -- or how did the conflict in Mostar differ from conflicts that you saw in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina or other parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think it differed in terms of what was going on at the time there. How do I turn the volume down again? Sorry. How is that? It's coming out really loud in my ears. Oh, okay. Yes, I think that's -- The way it differed, I think, was the intensity of what was happening. It was in a fairly limited geographical area, which probably magnified that. And also, I felt it was qualitatively different to what was going on, for example, at that time in Sarajevo, because it felt more cut off. There wasn't a black market. There weren't people in there getting rich, as there were in Sarajevo. In fact, what there was, was a highly mobilised population in the enclave on the east side which was absolutely dedicated to fighting the war, and you sometimes had the impression in other parts of the war in Yugoslavia, in the former Yugoslavia, that it was something that wasn't so intense at times. I mean, it was still very intense - don't get me wrong - but there was a higher degree of it, is what I'm trying to say, in Mostar at that particular time. I had also been in Vukovar in 1991 when it was being attacked by the Serbs and being shelled very heavily, and certainly the levels of destruction that I saw in parts of the Muslim-controlled parts of Mostar were as great as in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also at the beginning of the documentary, you stated that, roughly - I don't recall the exact words - I think you said that the HVO was aided and abetted by the Croatian army. Could you explain what you meant by that and why?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I can explain it on a number of different levels, really. The first of them -- sorry. It's just really loud in my ears. Where's the volume control? Okay. All right. I can live with it. It's all right, yes. Sorry. I can explain it on a number of different levels. There was evidence that I saw that there was an involvement by the Croatian army and, by extension, by the government in Zagreb, because I saw identity papers that had been taken from prisoners, from Croat prisoners, some of which were regular Croatian army IDs. Similar identities had also been taken from bodies. In addition, I spoke the previous autumn in -- yes, in 1992, September/October, to Dario Kordic in Busovaca, somewhere near there, you know, who was a well-connected Croat, who told me there was a connection with Zagreb. In addition, at the time, other journalists had looked into it and had seen a lot of connections there. Plus, some of the uniforms that members of the HVO were wearing were effectively the same as Croatian army uniforms. They even had very similar insignia, the very same style. It was a connection which -- I also spoke to people in Zagreb in an informal way who told me about it. So I think in all sorts of ways, it was clear there was a strong connection between the government in Zagreb and their ethnic brothers in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was footage that we saw, nighttime footage, of people walking across the foot bridge, across the river from West into East Mostar. Do you recall the date of that -- that that footage was taken?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that was September the 29th, 1993. We were filming that day in the east side of Mostar. We had a tip-off that it was happening, and we went down and filmed it. And I've also -- I've checked the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after that, the documentary showed some people you were talking to who had just entered East Mostar from the other side. What was the place where those interviews occurred?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The interviews took place in a -- a bombed out -- it was a theatre or a cinema that was in the centre of the enclave on the east side of Mostar. After those people crossed the river, they were taken up there by soldiers and were kept there certainly for that night. It seemed to be something of a reception centre - that was what it was being used as - where they took people and gave them their first night's shelter after they arrived in the east side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see people moving across from West Mostar at other times during either of those two periods which you spent in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On a number of different occasions I saw and I interviewed people who had crossed over from the west side of Mostar. On that night, that was when I saw the biggest single group. But also, you may recall from the documentary, the -- there was a scene where we were talking to some soldiers, and then some old people came. That was at another crossing point elsewhere. That was actually on the other side of the river, on the west side of the river, because we crossed the old bridge to get there and people would cross from there. Plus, in addition, in my trip there, my earlier trip in August, I met people who had -- Muslims who had come in from the -- some of the surrounding villages, surrounding villages - in this particular case, I think to the south of the enclave - and they all told the same kinds of stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim men, particularly Muslim men of military age, coming across from West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I saw no men of military age. The men that I saw were all old men and very, you know, old men. I would say 70-plus, late 60s. No one younger than that. The overwhelming majority of people who came over were women and children. I don't think I saw any boys above the age of-- I don't think I saw any boys who were reaching puberty, who were shaving. I would say maximum 11 or 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the footage that we saw was taken at the front line position on the west side of Mostar. Did any of the Armija, the Bosnian army soldiers, that you spoke to talk about HVO's use of Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I heard from a number of different sources a similar kind of story. It was that the Muslim prisoners would be used as human shields either in advance of an attack - mainly in advance of attacks, actually. Occasionally they talked about them having to do forced labour, building trenches, that kind of thing. But the stories that stood out were ones where they were -- there was one story where they said that Muslim prisoners had had to walk ahead of a tank that was moving up, also that they had been sent in front of attacks or they had been pushed into no man's land between the two front lines when on the HVO side there was some military activity going on. I heard that on two separate occasions from different people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the shelling. We saw shells falling, explosions happening in East Mostar. Could you talk about the frequency of the shelling when you were there and whether particular areas or positions were subject to more intense shelling than other areas?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The whole time that I was there on the two visits shelling was a pretty constant fact of life. Shelling could happen at any time. There really wasn't much of a pattern to it that I could discern. And you know, I had spent a long time in Sarajevo and in other places where there was shelling, so you would try and look for a pattern, because there would be times when it might be safer or not safe to go out. But in East Mostar, I could never see a particular pattern to it, and the shells could land anywhere. Shelling was -- there was always a chance essentially that everybody took when they went outside that they could -- that a mortar - generally mortars it would be - that a mortar shell could land and kill them. That's how the vast majority of the casualties that I saw received their wounds. A shell would land near them, and they would be killed or wounded by the fragmentation of the shell. There wasn't any pattern in terms of where they were landing or how often they were coming in or their frequency or their intensity. Sometimes there would be relatively calm periods for even a couple of hours, and then there would be a more intense period, you know. Like I say, you couldn't discern a pattern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sniping, could you describe the sniping activity and its effect on the population in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The prospect of being shot dead by a sniper was ever present for the civilian population there. There were places where it was impossible for it to happen because they were sheltered. But in basically all the main thoroughfares, there were places which people had to cross. There were places which you knew that if you were there, there was a chance of being sniped at. And in some places, there was a risk of being hit from two different directions. There was, for example - on the main road, I think it's Tito Street that runs from where the military headquarters was to where the hospital was, the war hospital was, which was a distance of probably total about 500 yards - there was a road junction which you would have to cross which you could be hit from two different directions there. Many people were killed around there. They put up signs saying: "Warning, sniper." And there was a way around the back going through someone's house in which you could avoid it. But sometimes, human beings being what they are, they would run across for whatever reason and often people would get hit. The effect of sniping was, in my opinion, to - not just my opinion, based on what I could see - was to terrorise the population. There was a constant fear of being hit by a sniper, which everybody who was in East Mostar at that particular time shared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Bowen, my last question: During the two time periods which you were in East Mostar filming, did the Bosnian authorities place any restrictions on where you could go, what you could film, and were there any restrictions, in fact, that you encountered in terms of where you could go and what you could do?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No. There were no restrictions placed on us by the Bosnian authorities there, by the civil authority, or by the military authorities, who were the people who really had power in the town at the time. We placed restrictions on ourselves, based on danger, based on not going to places where we weren't quite sure what was happening. We would always try to find some kind of a guide if we were trying to get to a front-line area, because I think it would have been foolhardy to go without one. But on the east side, where the bulk of the civilians were, we moved very freely. I got to know local people. I could walk around absolutely freely. We would go to people's houses. We didn't have a minder or a guide with us. As I say, we had guides going to front-line positions, but that's because we wanted them. At no time also while we were there in front-line positions did they say, "Don't film that, don't film this." We could do what we wanted. They also didn't place any restrictions on who we spoke to or what we said to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Seric. Cross-examined by Mr. Seric:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bowen. My name is Branko Seric, and I'm representing one of the accused in this case, Mr. Vinko Martinovic. At the beginning, I should like to ask you how you were able to reach East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: On the first trip when I went there in August, I linked up -- I had heard from the United Nations, from the UNHCR, that there was a way to get in with the Bosnian army, so I travelled from Sarajevo to Jablanica, and in Jablanica we made some inquiries. We linked up there with representatives of the Bosnian army who were staying at the hotel there - I think it's called the Hotel Bosna - and they explained to us that yes, they had a supply route that went from an area just south of Jablanica, on foot, across the mountains. It was a military supply route, effectively. And we asked if we could join one of these wagon trains of horses, mule trains, and they said yes, we could. We also linked up with a man called Humo, who was one of the commanders there. Coincidentally, he was in Jablanica, and he spoke good English, and he said he would show us where to go. So we linked up with them and walked in. That was in August. When we returned in September, we had contact with two British officials, one of whom worked for UNHCR, Jerrie Hulme, and one of whom worked for the EU monitoring group, Martin Garrod. They, between them - and Martin Garrod was particularly helpful - negotiated for us to enter the east side of Mostar in our own vehicle, following Garrod's vehicle. To get there, we crossed over the airport and drove in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I have to remind you that you have to speak very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The interpreters have some difficulties to follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll do my best. Do I need to repeat anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I thought I was speaking slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask for this overhead projector to be lowered down a little bit so that I could see the witness properly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please continue, Mr. Bowen. What happened after you went across to the eastern side of town in September?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: When we entered the east side of Mostar in September, nobody was expecting us. Because of the difficulties of the situation, it hadn't been possible to make a telephone call or anything like that. There were no telephones working, and as far as I know, nobody on that side had a satellite phone. Satellite phones at that time were much less common. So when we got into the east side of Mostar in September, we drove into the centre of the town. We came in in an armoured Land Rover. We then tried to link up with the people who I had got to know when I had been there in August. So we went first of all to the military headquarters, and I found Humo, the man who appears in the documentary. So I told them that we were there. I also went to the hospital and saw the doctor, who also appeared, the chief doctor, told him we were there, explained what we were doing. We found a place to stay, which was in a radio station that they had set up, and we set about doing our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated a moment ago that you had witnessed the enthusiasm of the BH army soldiers and how dedicated they were to their war effort. Esad Humo told you in front of the camera that even Alija Izetbegovic could sign a peace agreement, but as far as he was concerned, it meant nothing whatsoever to him. Could this statement be explained by what you have just told us about, that is, by his dedication to the war?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think he said not that Izetbegovic would sign a peace agreement and he wouldn't follow it. I think he said that if Izetbegovic decided that they would divide the city, then he wouldn't accept it. I felt that the motivation of people like Humo on that side came from the fact that they didn't believe that they had another choice. The vast majority of them had been civilians before that, and they had found themselves, as people had on all sides in the former Yugoslavia, they had found themselves in the military and they had to fight. And because of the particular circumstances on the east side of Mostar - it was a small enclave with a lot of civilians, quite a lot of fighting men as well - they were involved in what they believed at the time was a struggle for life and death. They thought it was very, very simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Mr. Bowen, but I think that we can achieve the objective of my cross-examination with answers even more brief. We saw a room in your film which contained some detained Croats. Do you know where that particular footage was filmed? Or let me put it directly to you: Was it the fourth elementary school which was located in the immediate vicinity of the health centre, or rather, the hospital that we saw on the film?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a school. I can tell you how it was filmed, because I was there. We had heard that they were holding prisoners. We asked if we could see them, and they agreed. So they took us into a building. It didn't seem to be like a school to me, I must say. It looked -- we were in a cellar, lower down, and it seemed more like a house or a commercial building. We went into the cellar. It wasn't particularly close to this medical centre, to the hospital, no. It was -- you know, the whole area was, anyway, quite small, but it was not in that immediate vicinity of the hospital. It was probably a few minutes' walk from it. But, you know, as I made the point in the film, in that enclave, nothing was more than a few minutes' walk away. If anything, it was closer to the military headquarters than to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We heard a comment in the film, something to the effect that you were not able to speak with the detainees. Was it that you were actually prohibited from talking to them, or were they prohibited from speaking to you in front of the cameras?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think it was more the second thing, that they were prohibited from talking to us. I did try -- I think also -- no, I think it was mainly that, that they were prohibited from talking to us. I did try to speak to one of them, and he just said nothing. He just looked down at the time. I don't recall if they told us not to speak to them. Perhaps they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were filming this particular portion of the footage, that is, the Croat detainees -- rather, when was it, if you remember, that you filmed the Croat detainees?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The Croat detainees who were filmed in the room underground were filmed during the second trip. The earlier pictures of Croat detainees where they were, if you remember, pictured exhuming bodies, digging up bodies, were filmed in August on my first trip there. That's right. And the picture also of the Croat detainee on the front line was filmed during the September trip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw Dr. Dragan Milavic in the film. While talking to him, or perhaps someone else, were you able to learn that every Croat detainee was made to give blood on a daily basis, and the quantity they took was 350 grams of blood per day, without their permission?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No. That's the first I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the film, you mentioned - I don't know whether it was you personally or someone else who was doing the soundtrack - that there were also Croats within the BH army. Did you have an opportunity to meet any such Croats on the -- in East Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I met Croats from the BH army in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that, perhaps, Slobodan Maric?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I don't remember that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the individual which has been indicted by this Tribunal. He's a fugitive from justice at the moment, but there's also an indictment against him in Mostar. Do you happen to know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with the case at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you must have done some research for your film, are you familiar with the fact that at the time you were making this film, that there were only seven Croats in East Mostar, whereas there were 9.000 Muslims living in West Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I did a lot of research based on the time that I was there, and I can tell you that I met many people, more than seven, who claimed to be either fully or partly ethnic Croat, people who were -- yeah, definitely, I met many more than seven. That comes -- that suggestion that there were only seven comes as a complete surprise to me. And it's not what I found. I found that there were many more than that and many people who said that they were either fully ethnically Croat or partly ethnically Croat from a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do any filming in Croat hospitals on the west side of Mostar where there were also dying civilians, the elderly, the wounded, women, children?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Not for this particular trip, no, because this film was about the east side. In the course of my time reporting the wars of former Yugoslavia, I filmed on all sides, but this particular film was about what was happening in one particular place at one particular time. So for this one, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And my final question: While you were walking about over there in East Mostar, did you see that the Muslims also had snipers who were targeting the other side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I didn't see snipers insofar as I didn't go to sniper positions with snipers using sniper rifles. However, the suggestion that they had snipers comes as no surprise to me. I would be very surprised if they didn't have snipers. Like I say, I didn't see them myself, but quite likely they had snipers. Certainly, they were firing at both sides. Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. I would like to introduce myself to you. I am Kresimir Krsnik, attorney at law, and I am Defence counsel for one of the accused here. I shall be very brief. I would just like to put a few questions to you. For the sake of impartiality, I believe that you can answer these questions, if you know the answers to them. You are an experienced war reporter according to all the rules of impartiality of your profession. I believe that you will agree with me on that, won't you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will also agree that images of war and suffering from war is not something foreign to you because you have seen that in many places that you reported from?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to answer the following question: Were you interested in the fate of non-Muslims who were in the territory that was under the absolute control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is the area that you travelled through from Jablanica to Mostar? I don't know if you've ever heard of Konjic. Did you investigate over there? Were you there doing your own journalistic work? Did you investigate what was going on in these territories that were under BH army control, that is, the area that you travelled through where you actually were?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The area I travelled through on that particular trip when I was heading from Sarajevo to Jablanica - and I have heard of Konjic, yes - I didn't stop to do journalistic investigations about what was happening en route. I would say, though, that in all the reporting that I did during the wars of former Yugoslavia, from 1991 right through to 1999 in Kosovo, I've always been interested in the plight of all civilians. In fact, that has been the main thrust of my reporting, of all different ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. Expecting this kind of answer, which is in line with your impartiality, your knowledge, and your professionalism and your work was unhindered, you never heard of the fourth elementary school in Mostar, which is a few steps away from the hospital that you filmed and it was one of the biggest camps for Croats in East Mostar and one of the major indictments of this Tribunal has to do with that? And also, over 30 detainees were killed there, and that has been established in proceedings before the Mostar court. And this is a minute's walk away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sorry, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you did your work, did you realise that? And especially when you were investigating civilians suffering and things like that, did you come across that as well? Were you aware of that? I'm just asking. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I had never heard while I was there of the fourth elementary school. I was aware that there were Croat detainees. And insofar as we could, we filmed that and put it in the documentary. The specifics of what was in the indictment though, no, I wasn't aware of that at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Distinguished witness, we will agree that the prisoners we saw on the film were prisoners of war, military prisoners. Or rather, can you explain to the Trial Chamber whether these were prisoners of war who were civilians or military personnel, whereas in the fourth elementary school that was a camp for civilian prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but I would caution against counsel inserting facts into the record which are not already in evidence, such as this fourth elementary school, and then building on that assertion in subsequent questions as though it is evidence. The fact is there's no evidence about the fourth elementary school that he is asking about that I can recall that has been presented at this stage during this trial. And so the witness has said he doesn't know anything about it. And I would respectfully suggest that that should be the end of the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In the film, we really saw some Croat prisoners, and we heard very clearly that the witness did not know anything about the so-called fourth elementary school. Mr. Krsnik, you may question about those prisoners, rather than to lead this witness to certain particular locations. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. My intention was very simple, I think, and it was easy to identify it as such. Was the witness aware of this or not? If not, we'll move on. But it had to do with what this witness said about the freedom of movement in Mostar, unrestricted at that. I absolutely had no other intention, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please be so kind as to tell me whether you know that the town of Mostar was shelled heavily during the Serb aggression. Do you know about the number of buildings - I shall restrict myself to buildings now only - were demolished during this shelling?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I know there had been earlier fighting there. My references to the intensity of the shelling were really based on what I saw while I was there. And while I was there, there was at times - not all of the time, but at times, as you saw in the film - there was intense shelling coming from the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that this will be my last question. You crossed the old bridge, as we saw on your film, so you came to the West Bank. Do you know the depth of BH army positions, in metres, kilometres, from the Neretva River to the delineation lines?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Not precisely in metres, but I know that -- my understanding was that the front line was in a road called Bulevar, and it wasn't a very -- it wasn't a very long distance, though at times like that, of course, moving a short distance is very difficult. But I knew -- I could see on the map where it was. It was shown to me. We went out to it as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you that, sir, because of another question I'm trying to get to, and I would like to shorten this cross-examination as much as possible. Do you remember a long line of buildings, apartment buildings, going to the Neretva River which were a kind of shelter, viewed from the Neretva? If you wish, I can even give you a map, if that would make it easier for you. I'm asking you all of this -- I mean, of course we are not treating you as a classical witness here. This is a conversation, to put it that way, or at least I am treating you in that way. I'm asking you this because when I saw the picture of that poor woman lying by the Neretva and I saw the bridge too, and you were passing there -- and it is practically impossible to have sniper fire there, because there are many buildings there that are sort of like a shield, and those buildings were held by the BH army. So that's my question. That is the purpose of my question. Did you see that and did you pass there? Or perhaps I can make this even shorter. Do you personally know that she was killed by sniper fire, or did somebody tell you about this? Let me be as brief as possible. Let me limit my questions to a minimum and not to bother you with maps and things like that. That would be my question, then.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: She was killed by a bullet, not by shrapnel. As for the apartments, I don't remember those apartments. In fact, my recollection of where that woman was was that it was a fairly open area which has -- it's not very built up around there, in fact, in the area where she was shot. So I don't recall those apartments, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it can also be seen on your footage, the Hotel Ruza on the other side. Of course, it's demolished, and it was held by the BH army. It's on the other side of the river, but it can be seen on your footage: the Ruza Hotel, the buildings, and also the old bridge on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel now is not putting any questions to the witness; he's just arguing with the witness - that's my suggestion - based on images he saw on the footage. I think that he should put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Where could that bullet have come from, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: If you remember the shot, the picture of the woman, the image you saw I think just before it was of the hotel, but the actual location was somewhere -- wasn't directly opposite it, is what I'm saying. That's the first thing. The second thing is: My assumption in these things is that if a civilian -- I don't believe that they were shooting their own people, if that's what you're trying to say. I don't believe that the woman was shot by a Muslim sniper at the time. Sure, I couldn't do a ballistics examination of the bullet, but I felt, based on what was going on there at the time, based on a pattern of behaviour which I could discern as a journalist, that it was a fair assumption to make that the shot came from the western side of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness. That's precisely what I wanted to hear. This is an assumption, a fair assumption. Because we heard even in your film that a man admitted that he had to throw a grenade among his own people. It's times of war; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just have a second, Your Honours, please? Because my colleague says that she has some suggestions. I do apologise. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Distinguished Witness, we have heard Mr. Humo's views. You have talked to Mr. Pasalic -- or rather, have you talked to Mr. Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what he was fighting for and what kind of a state he wanted to have?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Did he? I'm trying to recall. Hang on. With Pasalic, I spoke more about directly military, strategic matters. I don't recall him giving his views on what particular state that he wanted after the war or what he was fighting for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience and your tours of various theaters of war, do you think that a general could refuse orders issued by a higher command? In this case, it's Sarajevo, and we heard this in your film, that he did not obey orders from Sarajevo and that he didn't care about orders from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's the comment that was heard as he was walking up the hill of Hum. But then the witness is here. He can say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you are asking the opinions from this witness rather than the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. You're right. I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: When you were in East Mostar - this is my last question - there was arms trading with the Serbs or tanks [as interpreted], and tank crews were rented out from them, and heavy weapons. Did you actually see that as you toured the area?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I didn't see Serb troops, but I was told by various people there that they were doing deals with the Serbs, that they were buying weapons from the Serbian -- the Serb side. As for renting heavy weapons, I never heard about that. The kind of things that I saw were lighter weapons, mainly Kalashnikovs and RPGs. Could I just answer -- you didn't give me a chance to answer the assertions you were making too about this assumption about where the bullet was coming from, because you -- before I could answer, you spoke to your colleague. Could I address that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that in covering a war, of course you can't be at all times -- when you see the consequences of a shot, you can't always be where the shot was fired from. When I used the word "assumption," maybe it was the wrong word. What I really meant was deduction. You have to deduce from the balance of probabilities in a situation what happened, based not just on that situation but on the kinds of things that were going on over a period of time. That was why we came to the conclusions that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were all the questions that the Defence had for you. Thank you very much for your answers, sir, and also for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for helping us by giving your evidence. Is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just a very few questions. Re-examined by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you mentioned that you reported on the conflict in Vukovar in 1991, I believe. Just so we all know, what country is Vukovar located in?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Vukovar is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the victims of the crimes that were taking place in Vukovar when you were there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Croatians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report on that as a journalist for the BBC?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did extensively report on the situation of Croatians in 1991. Actually not just in Vukovar but in other places as well like Kozjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My final question: Why didn't you make a film or a documentary about what was happening in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity. I would very much have liked to have had that opportunity to do it. I think it was a very interesting situation. We did try and -- my team - not me personally - did try to make some overtures to the Bosnian Croat authorities on the west side of Mostar, but they were rebuffed. They wouldn't let us work there with the freedom that we had on the other side. So therefore, there was an idea, as I say, to do one, but it didn't come off because we basically weren't allowed to work freely there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Judge Clark. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, it must have been fairly harrowing for you to view that film again after all these years, as I think it was very harrowing for all of us to watch. I have a question to ask in relation to the geography of the place which is not clear to me. East Mostar appears to have been a surrounding enclave that was being bombarded morning, noon, and night, as you said. What was the situation on the east side of Mostar? Were there Croats there, or was that Serbian territory? Further east.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Further east there was Serbs, but my understanding was that they -- the enclave was completely surrounded by the Bosnian Croats. However, on the east side of the enclave, the lines were a bit more porous. It was possible to get through in different places either to connect up with the Serbs or to connect up with their route they took to get out to Jablanica. So I mean it was a bona fide siege insofar as people couldn't get out. It was just the military men, as I say, could find a way out through the front lines on the north and to the north and north-east, was my understanding certainly, because that was where I came in. Whether it was possible elsewhere, I don't know because I wasn't -- I didn't try and do it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I was just wondering what was the attitude of the Serbs to the population of Mostar - do you know? - during this critical period.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I think my understanding of the official attitude of the Serb side was they were quite happy to see Croats and Muslims fighting each other. And you know, it suited them to see that going on. And for whatever reason, for reasons of their own, they didn't intervene except to stir the pot a little bit by selling weapons to one side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was there any question of humanitarian aid coming into East Mostar from the eastern end?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The only humanitarian aid that I saw come in came in UN convoys. Throughout this whole time, there were Spanish UNPROFOR troops who were present in the town. And in August, while I was there, the first convoy from the UNHCR came in. And after that, there was limited access. Convoys would come in sometimes, but that was all United Nations stuff. There wasn't anything coming from any of the other sides there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could you see any evidence of humanitarian aid being prevented from coming to the aid of East Mostar by any authority? And if you did see that, perhaps you could describe it.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: The only evidence I have on that is based on conversations with Jerrie Hulme who was one of the -- he was basically in charge of the UNHCR there. He was basically their senior man who had come in to Mostar. I didn't ask him, to be honest with you, about the detail of the negotiations, but he said that there were a lot of holdups in the -- that they would like to run regular aid convoys in to Mostar because there were major humanitarian needs there. But they weren't able to do it because it took a massive amount of negotiation to get the supplies in, which came up from the Croatian coast. And they came up from -- I think the road would come past Medjugorje in the Croat-controlled area, and then in that way. So he talked about the complexity of the negotiations and how difficult it was. But I mean, like I say, I didn't talk to him in sort of blow by blow about who did what and when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of the Judge's question? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only one question related to Judge Clark's question. Again, this is a question of geography. I would also like to have this clarified. So if the Trial Chamber agrees, perhaps we could try to clarify the situation with this witness. So in that case, I would like to ask the Registry for Exhibit P2, please. I think that that is the easiest way of proceeding as far as geography is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Have you got the right map this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I always try to make sure whether Stolac is there or not, but I still have the other map, too, Your Honours, without Stolac. It's still in the binder. Further cross-examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, perhaps it would not be a bad thing if you took the map into your hands so that you could see it more closely. It would be easier to communicate that way, I think. Can you see Mostar there? Can you see an orange line leading to Jablanica, and then going in two directions, Jablanica and Sarajevo, and then another one going to Prozor? That's the road; right? Further up.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course, it's clear, Sarajevo, and then you have to go to Jablanica and to Konjic. That's the way you had to travel. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Jablanica then Konjic -- no, I don't think we went to Konjic. When we travelled from Sarajevo to Jablanica, what happened was we came down the main road from Sarajevo up to, you know -- and I can't remember the exact point, because the road was cut. And then we had to go -- if you see, there's a lake. My recollection is that we went up through a forest from that road through some very windy forest tracks. And then we crossed over, I think it was a railway bridge actually, which was being used also for road traffic, because the BH army didn't control the whole of the main road. So it was quite easy to drive down from -- once we got on to the road out of Sarajevo, it was quite easy to drive down until the road was cut, which was somewhere near Konjic. And I don't recall whether it was in Konjic or before Konjic. And then we went up and around to Jablanica, and from Jablanica -- the trail where we walked started at Glogosnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Witness, this is September 1993, and you are trying to say that this municipality here, the municipality of Konjic, the municipality of Jablanica, and now this road going from Mostar to Jablanica, that that was not under BH control throughout?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was not under their control, no, because we walked with them across the mountains. It took 20 hours, and their soldiers were walking there, too. I'm sure if the road was open, they would have used it. No. I mean I also heard from the UN that the only way in was through this mountain track across those hills from Glogosnica down to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to the best of your recollection, from this road here - and now I'm looking towards the west, Konjic, Jablanica, towards Konjic and Jablanica - this was not territory -- I mean all the way up to Mostar. Actually, to the right, or if you want, to the east of the Neretva River, going parallel to the road, because the road follows the Neretva up to Jablanica, and then there is this little lake called Neretvica because of the hydroelectric power plant there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to this question and this line of questions which is, I believe, beyond the scope of the questioning made by Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Are you doubting that this witness has never been to this place? What's the relevance to the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, certainly not. The relevance is -- I'll tell you straight away. First I wanted to handle this whole thing geographically. We are -- we will try to prove during our Defence case that in September, Mostar was not an enclave. I just wanted to help the Court at this point, to clarify this from a geographical point of view. Nothing else. I wanted to do this for the Trial Chamber. And if the Trial Chamber thinks this is not necessary, then I will put no further questions. Then I'm finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I'm amazed at what you just said. This journalist, who has spent six weeks, I think, in Mostar, has given evidence for quite a while, and we've seen his film describing Mostar as an enclave, and he's clarified for me that there was no freedom on the east side, and you now say that it's going to be your defence case that Mostar was not an enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, that's what the translation says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. No. You could take a road, Vrapcici, Potoci, and Prigradjani, and that the BH army held that under their control. That is a historical fact. And then I asked the witness further than that. That's the only thing I want to clarify, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, then, you should have put those questions in direct examination specifically to Mr. Bowen, because he's in a position to refute it. It's not the time, at the end of the case, to bring your witnesses to prove something that has never been put, because this Trial Chamber won't like it then. You must put your case to the specific witnesses when they're here, not when they've left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour. My apologies to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the road leading from Mostar, and then via the village of Vrapcici, which is the first one on the orange line, the next one being Potoci, and so on - so looking from where we are now, it would have been on the right bank of the Neretva, along the road which runs parallel to the river - did you use that particular road in the month of September 1993 to enter and exit the area of East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I don't recall the name -- as I said in the film, we went to the northern -- we went to the northern edge of the enclave, to some of the outlying villages, which was the place where -- unfortunately, I don't have my notebook with me, so I don't have the precise names, otherwise I would be able to tell you. But that was the place where I had arrived with the Bosnian army in August, when I had walked from Glogosnica, near Jablanica. And it was possible to get by car about, I'd say, approximately 4 or 5 miles out of town to the north, but it was a contested road, where we were fired on. That's where they had the searchlights. Both times I went down that road -- in August, when I travelled over it with the Bosnian army in one of their trucks, we were fired on, and when I went out there in the BBC vehicle, to the edge of it, we were also fired on, in both directions, coming in and going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for helping us by giving your evidence. We wish you a good trip back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to attend? Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender the videotape documentary which is marked as Exhibit 586. English -- I'm sorry. We have transcripts of the videotape as well, both in English and French, which have been in the booths, and a French version could also be made available to Judge Diarra if she wishes to have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This videotape has been admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm informed that I should -- apparently the transcripts have also been given exhibit numbers, and so that would be Exhibit 587 would be the English and French transcript of the documentary, and so we tender those also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that those transcripts will go with that videotape. Without that videotape, certainly we will not admit that transcript alone. So we had better have another type of the numbering, for instance, a slash, you know, 1 or 2, or certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the videotape itself is marked as Exhibit 586, and then the transcripts are marked as Exhibit 587, so that they do have different exhibit numbers, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections? Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, but we also expect the Croatian translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber has made decisions concerning the translations of the B/C/S version. We believe that the transcripts of this videotape is within the scope of that incidence, which I mean that it's within the time frame of what happened during that period, so that should be translated into the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've been informed that in fact it has been translated and it will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any number for that translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would propose to simply add that to Exhibit 587, which already consists of the English and the French language transcripts, so that then 587 could also include the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So document P587 is admitted into evidence. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in the spirit of this Trial Chamber's ruling on the translation of documents and exhibits to be admitted, we were not provided the Serbo-Bosnian-Croatian or Croatian transcript prior to the tape being shown. In the future, we would appreciate it if the Prosecutor would give us the translated documents prior to the witness's testimony so that our clients could review those prior to it. As you see now, we will get them later and our client will be able to look at them, but Mr. Bowen will be in London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that if a translation exists, the Prosecutor will do his best to provide those translations beforehand, so that to facilitate your client to understand the contents of that videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm informed the B/C/S version was contained in the 17 binders that were distributed to the Defence prior to the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now shall we have the previous witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It was a closed-session witness, but we would be prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
